sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

sections.content: 2 The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents 1. Introduction Multimodal foundation models have rapidly advanced in understanding, reasoning, and generation across text, images, video, and audio [112], enabling agents to perceive, decide, and act in open environments [1315]. We view multimodal intelligence as an evolving loop: worlds provide tasks, humans guide learning, and agents interact with the world to produce verifiable outcomes [16, 17]. As tasks and environments grow increasingly complex, this loop faces two bottlenecks: (1) Constructing large-scale, heterogeneous, and verifiable environments manually is costly, motivating automated world generation; and (2) Agent capability is increasingly constrained by the Harness [1823], whose manual iteration cannot keep pace with growing task complexity and diversity. Inspired by Harness recursive self-improvement [2426] and agentenvironment co-evolution [27 29], we ask whether this manual loop can improve continuously. Generated worlds provide adaptive curricula, while verified interaction feedback guides Harness updates. However, extending this process across heterogeneous text-only and multimodal tasks [30, 31] presents challenge. Current Harness RSI works focus on text-modality tasks (e.g., coding and math [23, 24, 32, 33]) and adopt task-specific evolution [22, 25, 34, 35]. This approach is suitable when tasks share similar capability requirements, but can lead to Harness overfitting and poor generalization across heterogeneous tasks. Conversely, global Harness struggles to accommodate conflicting task demands, including performanceefficiency trade-offs in embodied tasks, limiting its efficiency and adaptability. key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. For example, although ARC-AGI-3 [36] and Micromouse [37] differ in task structure, both rely on accurate perception and state tracking: the former requires recognizing grid states and their changes, while the latter requires continuously updating environmental information during maze exploration. Grouping tasks by these shared capability requirements makes the underlying mechanisms common learning objective, enabling generalization across tasks. Position. Current RSI training relies heavily on task-specific optimization, limiting capability generalization across tasks. We advocate shift from task-driven to capability-driven selfimprovement, where shared capability requirements across tasks guide the learning and optimization of multiple specialized Harnesses. This shift highlights the role of shared capabilities in cross-task generalization and naturally motivates capability-aware Router that matches tasks to suitable Harnesses based on their capability requirements. To operationalize this position, we introduce The Trinity, recursive self-improvement framework coupling environment generation with agent evolution through Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Using verified trajectories, Evolver identifies task capability requirements and groups tasks sharing them, reorganizing the original task tree into hierarchical capability tree. Heterogeneous tasks at the same node share learning objective, motivating Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable environments, while evaluation on the original tasks measures capability transfer. Along the capability tree, Explorer evolves Harness tree through selective inheritance and local refinement, while Creator evolves at corresponding nodes and consolidates validated updates into new Base Harness at the end of each iteration. The Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, requiring task-dependent selection. For Explorer, our Capability-Aware Harness Router uses verified execution experience and public task information to select matching branch of Explorers Harness tree. For Creator, overlap within its Harness tree motivates merging complementary modules and removing near-duplicates to form new Base Harness. Explorer and Creator play distinct roles in RSI processes along the same capability tree. 3 The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents Contributions. ❶ Capability-driven multimodal RSI. We make shared capability requirements the organizing principle of Harness evolution. Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real turns these requirements into compact training worlds, yielding reusable module-based Harness tree whose specialization motivates capability-aware routing. ❷ Capabilitymodule priors for Harness design. We connect task-level capability requirements to reusable module configurations, using empirical associations and controlled interventions to examine which module support matters for task. ❸ Efficient evolution and transfer. We show that targeting shared decision logic supports effective Harness improvement at low evolution cost, with transfer across heterogeneous tasks, unseen benchmarks, and real-world embodied settings. 2. Preliminaries 2.1. Multimodal Agentic Tasks Long-horizon multimodal agentic tasks span interactive games [38], GUI manipulation [39], and embodied interaction [13, 14]. They combine perception, understanding, reasoning, and generation with memory, planning, and adaptation across observationaction sequences. Agents must retain evidence, revise hypotheses, and adjust plans as observations arrive. Because later decisions depend on earlier actions and feedback, misread observations or forgotten constraints can propagate across steps. Agent performance thus increasingly depends on effective Harness organization and coordination. Dynamically coordinating capabilities over long interactions and adapting to increasingly large, heterogeneous task sets remain key challenges. 2.2. The evaluated Harnessskill configurations improve on both simulated and physical tasks, linking node-level module evolution with task-specific skill preparation. 5. Related Work Recursive Harness Self-Improvement. Self-improvement spans Gödel machines [87], LLM systems that rewrite their own agent code [24, 88, 89], automated agent design [9092], prompt optimization [9395], and learning from self-feedback and reflection [9698]. With weights fixed, improvement shifts to the harness, which is synthesized from environment feedback [33], repaired from failed trajectories [32, 35], self-revised [19], optimized as code [18, 20], adapted at test time [99] or per task [22], improved at the meta level [100, 101], and shown to lift frozen MLLMs [21]; benchmarks and surveys map this space [23, 102, 103]. Closest to ours are JIT-Agents harness generator [25], HarnessXs typed primitives [104], HSIs per-task-family harnesses [34], ModularRSIs modules evolved on benchmark-disjoint tasks [26], and the flat capability map of Harness Continual Learning [105] and regime-branched harness tree of Adaptive Auto-Harness [106], both evolved on the task stream. Trinity instead induces capability tree from training trajectories, shares prefixes across 44 heterogeneous benchmarks with selective module inheritance, evolves Harnesses in Creator-generated worlds that exclude target-task layouts and solutions, and evaluates on held-out benchmarks and real robots. Unlike LLM routers [40], ours routes among capability-specific Harnesses over one frozen backbone. Co-evolution of Agents and Environments. Open-ended co-evolution [107109], unsupervised environment design [29, 110], curricula [111, 112], and embodied co-design [28] adapt training to the learner; Voyager grows skill library under an automatic curriculum [113]. Loops co-evolve language agents with environments [114], optimizers [115], or harnesses [116, 117]; environment generation spans embodied [118, 119], tool-use [120], and terminal settings [121, 122], language world models [123], and game verification [124]. SPADE is closest [27]: one LLM designs environments with verification code and learns roles by reinforcement learning. Trinity keeps the backbone frozen and couples world generation with Explorer and Creator Harness evolution along capability The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents hierarchy, execution outcomes refining Explorer and verifier-detected failures refining Creator. 6. Conclusion We advocate Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement and introduce The Trinity, framework that couples world generation with Harness evolution through Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. By organizing heterogeneous tasks around shared capability requirements, the framework constructs simplified, verifiable worlds whose execution feedback guides the evolution of reusable modules. These modules form specialized Harness configurations, with capabilitymodule correlations and controlled interventions providing empirical support for capability requirements as priors for module design and composition. To apply these evolved capabilities across tasks, capability-aware routing selects suitable Harness configurations using public task information and verified execution experience. Experiments across diverse training and unseen benchmarks demonstrate improved aggregate performance and cross-task generalization, while deployment in two real-world embodied settings further illustrates the transfer of these capabilities to physical environments. 7. Discussion Limitations. Our framework uses web search for benchmark discovery, but retrieval coverage and result quality may vary across queries. In addition, our current study focuses primarily on selfimprovement at the Harness level. Outlook. Capability-driven learning offers new paradigm for generalizable agent improvement, where shared capability requirements across tasks guide learning and optimization. Our framework and results at the Harness level demonstrate the promise of this perspective. Looking ahead, we envision dynamically expanding the capability tree to capture emerging capability requirements and extending this paradigm to model parameter training, where capability-aware routing and RSI form closed loop that jointly drives capability discovery, acquisition, and refinement. 8. Candidate benchmarks were collected through agent web search over five types of source: research benchmarks released with code or data, public AI competitions, human contests and testing standards, published games and puzzle communities, and professional practice. Because multimodal agent must perceive its world through whatever interface that world exposes, the inventory spans every input modality in which agentic tasks are posed, and each benchmark retains the observation protocol of its source. Each modality probes different part of an agents capability. Image input (photographs, rendered scenes, puzzle images, and robot camera views) tests perception from pixels, viewpoint selection, and the grounding of decisions in what is seen. Video input tests evidence acquisition over time: selecting frames within budget, tracking events across them, and understanding what 25 The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents happened. Boards, grids, and maps rendered as text test spatial reasoning and state tracking over symbolic visual state; with pixel-level perception removed, failure can be attributed to reasoning rather than to seeing. Plain text tests the capabilities multimodal agent relies on downstream of perception: rule discovery, experimental design, planning, negotiation, and strategic interaction. Keeping all four modalities in one inventory lets visual and text benchmarks share nodes in the capability tree (Appendix B). Nine of the training sources publish their rules but provide no agent-facing environment: Chess Tactics [50], Eleusis [41], Euro NCAP AEB [63], Master Keying [55], Micromouse [37], Pallet Rack Inspection [60], Saboteur [73], The Long Dark [81], and WCA Cube Solving [53] (marked * in Figure 9). We rebuilt each of them through agent web search from the published rules and examples, preserving the mechanics, information access, and scoring of the source; the rebuilt environments present their state to the agent as images or symbolic text. Embodied Benchmarks The simulation of each embodied benchmark runs in an environment built from its real scene, which closely reproduces the layout and furnishings of the site, with model of the same robot as the real runs: Unitree G1 for SOON and an AlohaMini2 for CaP-X. For SOON we rebuilt the office from its floor plan and from photographs and video of the site: the side room where the robot starts, the doorway into the office, the rows of desks with their chairs and cabinets, and the white pedestal fan beside the target desk. The office is 3D scene in which the walls and furniture are collision obstacles: each action moves the robot by the nominal distance or angle of the real robots motion profile, move that hits an obstacle counts as collision and ends the episode as failure, and after every action the agent receives the head-camera image rendered from the robots new pose with the height, downward pitch, and field of view of the real camera. On the real robot person judges every episode on site, and an episode in which the robot collides with an obstacle is failure. The G1 starts in the side room, walks through the doorway into the office, and must stop at the desk next to the white fan and touch it within 30 movement actions. For CaP-X we built the table scene in the MuJoCo physics simulator [125] with the official AlohaMini2 model, and with objects of the same size and colour as the real ones: three paper cups, 9 cm tall, 7 cm across the mouth, and 5 cm across the closed bottom, stand upside down on white table, and in most layouts 2 cm cube, red, green, or blue, lies under one of them. The AlohaMini2 stands at the near edge of the table with its two six-joint arms; its mobile base and lift stay still. After every action the agent sees the head camera, the wrist cameras on both grippers, and fixed side camera; it moves gripper in small steps while the host solves the arms inverse kinematics, and within 30 actions it must report whether cube is present and, if it is, its colour and the cup it is under.
